scenario: AITA for not helping a woman at walmart | I (male 24) started working at walmart for the summer about a month ago. My job mainly involves working with inventory in the back room and not on the floor with customers, sometimes we get heavy boxes that we need to lift as a part of our regular duties. One of my co-workers is a female (fcw) in her early to mid 30s, physically in good shape and as far as I can tell no physical disabilities. (Fcw) approaches me and asks if I can help her lift a heavy box, I say of course and I walk over to the box with her expecting us to perform a team lift - however we get to the box and as I get to one side of the box expecting her to go to the other she just stands there and watches me. I ask "are you ready?" And she says "yes it just needs to go in that bin" (referencing a metal shelving unit about 4 feet high). I say "ok let's do it" and she responds "it's to heavy for me can you please lift it into the bin?". I respond by saying "I'm more than happy to help anyone if they're having trouble with something, but I'm not going to lift all your heavy boxes for you while you stand there watching me" and (fcw) said "if you're not willing to help me I'll find someone who will" and stormed off. Later on the head guy on our team (not my boss just the guy with most seniority who directs us) walks up to me and said " I just spoke to (fcw), the next time someone asks for help you need to help them, that's part of being a team. I responded by clarifying exactly what happened in case she stretched the truth and finished by saying "we're both paid to do the exact same job and if she cant perform the tasks then she shouldn't have taken the job, I'm not the designated heavy lifter on our team and if you would like to discuss this further we can do it with HR present", and at this point feeling pretty annoyed, it was my turn to storm off. So, was I the asshole in this situation? Because so far it seems like its 2 against 1.

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I was the asshole in this situation at Walmart. Let me start by going through what happened step by step. First, I've been working at Walmart for about a month, mainly in the backroom dealing with inventory. My job involves lifting heavy boxes as part of regular duties. One of my coworkers is a woman in her early to mid-30s, who seems physically fit and doesn't have any obvious disabilities. One day, this coworker approached me and asked if I could help her lift a heavy box. I agreed and walked over to the box with her, expecting us to do a team lift. But when we got to the box, she just stood there watching me instead of helping. I asked, "Are you ready?" and she said, "Yes, it just needs to go in that bin." I said, "Okay, let's do it," and she responded, "It's too heavy for me. Can you please lift it into the bin?" I told her, "I'm more than happy to help anyone if they're having trouble with something, but I'm not going to lift all your heavy boxes for you while you stand there watching me." She got upset and said, "If you're not willing to help me, I'll find someone who will," and stormed off. Later, the head guy on our team, who's not my boss but the most senior person directing us, walked up to me and said, "I just spoke to [FCW], and the next time someone asks for help, you need to help them. That's part of being a team." I responded by clarifying exactly what happened in case she stretched the truth and finished by saying, "We're both paid to do the exact same job, and if she can't perform the tasks, then she shouldn't have taken the job. I'm not the designated heavy lifter on our team, and if you would like to discuss this further, we can do it with HR present." Feeling pretty annoyed, it was my turn to storm off. So, was I the asshole in this situation? It seems like it's two against one, with the head guy and the coworker against me. First, I need to understand the expectations of the job. We're both paid to do the same job, which includes lifting heavy boxes. It's part of our regular duties. So, if she can't perform the tasks, she shouldn't have taken the job. That makes sense. But she asked for help, and I agreed to help. However, when we got to the box, she didn't help. She just stood there and then asked me to lift it alone. That seems unfair. I was willing to help, but I expected her to do her part too. When she said it was too heavy for her, I told her I was happy to help if she was having trouble, but I wasn't going to lift all her heavy boxes for her. That seems reasonable. I was setting boundaries. She got upset and said she'd find someone else to help. Then the head guy told me I needed to help her next time. I explained the situation and stood my ground, saying I wasn't the designated heavy lifter and that if she couldn't do the job, she shouldn't have taken it. Feeling annoyed, I stormed off. So, was I the asshole? It seems like I was just trying to set boundaries and not take on extra work that wasn't my responsibility. But the head guy and the coworker seem to think I should have helped her without expecting her to do her part. Maybe I should have been more understanding and helped her without expecting her to lift. But I was already lifting heavy boxes as part of my job. If I had to lift all her boxes too, that would be more than my share. Alternatively, maybe I should have communicated better. Instead of saying I wasn't going to lift all her boxes, I could have said something like, "I'm happy to help, but let's do it together." That way, I'm still setting boundaries but in a more constructive way. Also, when the head guy told me to help her next time, I could have acknowledged his concern and suggested that we work together as a team, rather than storming off. In the end, it seems like both sides have valid points. I was trying to set boundaries and not take on extra work, but I could have communicated more effectively and worked as a team. The head guy and the coworker might feel that I was being uncooperative and not part of the team. So, maybe I was a bit of an asshole in how I communicated and set boundaries, but I also had valid concerns about not taking on extra work that wasn't my responsibility. I think the key takeaway is that communication is important, and setting boundaries should be done respectfully and constructively, rather than in a way that makes others feel unsupported or unappreciated. In the future, I could work on communicating my boundaries more clearly and constructively, while also being open to working as a team and supporting my coworkers when needed.
